```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 3.5
)
```

```{r}
#| label: load-packages
library(ggseg)
library(ggplot2)
```

You have the plot.
The colours say what they need to say.
And then someone in the room asks which blob is the insula.

That is what `geom_brain_text()` is for.
It writes a region's name onto the region, and `geom_brain_label()` puts the name in a box — the same pair ggplot2 gives you with `geom_text()` and `geom_label()`.

## The layer already knows which brain it is labelling

Add it after a `geom_brain()` layer and it takes that layer's atlas, layout, hemisphere and view.
You do not say any of it twice, and the labels cannot drift onto a different brain from the one you drew.

```{r}
#| label: label-everything
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Left lateral view of the dk atlas with all 34 region names written
#|   across it in small text. Several names overlap where regions are narrow.
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Every region named at once. It works, and it shows you why you will
#|   usually want fewer.
ggplot() +
  geom_brain(
    atlas = dk(), hemi = "left", view = "lateral", show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_brain_text(size = 2.5) +
  theme_brain2()
```

That is every region the layer drew, and it is honestly a bit of a mess.
Thirty-four names on one view only just fit, and `banks of superior temporal sulcus` has to go somewhere.
On a parcellation with hundreds of regions this is not a thing you can do at all.

So most of the time you want a handful of names, not all of them.

## Naming a few regions

Subsetting is `data`, the same as any other ggplot2 layer.
Hand the label layer a data frame holding the regions you want named, keyed on `label` or on `region` — the same keys `brain_join()` uses.

```{r}
#| label: label-some
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Left lateral view of the dk atlas with only two regions named: insula
#|   and precentral, each written on its own region.
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Two names instead of thirty-four, chosen by handing the layer less data.
ggplot() +
  geom_brain(
    atlas = dk(), hemi = "left", view = "lateral", show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_brain_text(
    data = data.frame(label = c("lh_insula", "lh_precentral")),
    size = 4
  ) +
  theme_brain2()
```

Your own columns come along for the ride, so the text does not have to be the region's name.
Map `label` to whatever the data carries.

```{r}
#| label: label-mapping
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Left lateral view of the dk atlas where the insula is annotated with the
#|   text p < .001 and the precentral gyrus with n.s.
#| fig-cap: "The text is whatever your data says, not necessarily the anatomy."
findings <- data.frame(
  label = c("lh_insula", "lh_precentral"),
  note = c("p < .001", "n.s.")
)

ggplot() +
  geom_brain(
    atlas = dk(), hemi = "left", view = "lateral", show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_brain_text(data = findings, aes(label = note), size = 4) +
  theme_brain2()
```

## Where the name actually lands

Not in the middle of the region, which is the first thing you would reach for and the thing that quietly breaks.
A crescent or horseshoe region has its centre outside itself, so the name ends up printed on a neighbour.
That is not a rare edge case: it is true of 9% of the shapes in `dk` and 41% of those in `tracula`.

Instead the name goes on the widest run of region that a horizontal line crosses, which is inside the shape by construction.
A region drawn in several views gets named in each of them, on its largest piece, and the grey backdrop never gets named because it is not a region.

## Moving a name off a small region

Plenty of regions are too small or too narrow to hold their own name, and that is the normal case rather than the exception.
`nudge_x` and `nudge_y` move a label in atlas units — the same units as the axes, so for a `dk` view about 215 units across, 40 is a visible shift.

The nice part is that you only say where to move it.
The leader line back to the region and the justification both follow from the nudge.

```{r}
#| label: nudge
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Left lateral view of the dk atlas with three names placed outside the
#|   brain outline: superior frontal above left, temporal pole below left,
#|   lateral occipital to the right. A thin line runs from each name to its
#|   region.
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Three names nudged clear of the outline. Each turns to face away from
#|   its region, and each keeps a line back to it.
ggplot() +
  geom_brain(
    atlas = dk(), hemi = "left", view = "lateral", show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_brain_text(
    data = data.frame(
      label = c("lh_superiorfrontal", "lh_temporalpole", "lh_lateraloccipital")
    ),
    nudge_x = c(-70, -40, 90),
    nudge_y = c(70, -55, -20),
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  coord_brain(clip = "off") +
  theme_brain2()
```

Watch out for `coord_brain(clip = "off")` there.
Without it, a label pushed past the edge of the panel is cut off at the edge, and you will spend a while wondering why your nudge did nothing.

Each nudge belongs to the row you wrote it next to.
Leave one at `0` and that label is drawn plainly on its region with no line at all, so a single layer can mix the two.

```{r}
#| label: nudge-some
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Left lateral view of the dk atlas where insula is written directly on
#|   its region with no line, while temporal pole sits below the outline with
#|   a line running back to it.
#| fig-cap: >
#|   A label left at zero gets no line. The connector appears because
#|   something moved, not because you asked for it.
ggplot() +
  geom_brain(
    atlas = dk(), hemi = "left", view = "lateral", show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_brain_text(
    data = data.frame(label = c("lh_insula", "lh_temporalpole")),
    nudge_x = c(0, -40),
    nudge_y = c(0, -40),
    size = 4
  ) +
  coord_brain(clip = "off") +
  theme_brain2()
```

## Tuning the leader line

The gaps at either end are yours to set.
`box.padding` is the gap next to the text and `point.padding` the gap next to the region, both in grid units.
`min.segment.length` is the length below which no line is drawn at all, which keeps a barely-moved label from sprouting a useless stub.
`segment.colour` and `segment.linewidth` style the line itself.
Left alone, a line takes the colour of its own text, so you rarely have to think about it.

```{r}
#| label: leader-style
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Left lateral view of the dk atlas with superior temporal named in a
#|   boxed label below the brain, joined by a grey line with a wide gap at
#|   both ends.
#| fig-cap: >
#|   A boxed label with roomier padding and a grey line, using
#|   geom_brain_label().
ggplot() +
  geom_brain(
    atlas = dk(), hemi = "left", view = "lateral", show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_brain_label(
    data = data.frame(label = "lh_superiortemporal"),
    nudge_x = -30,
    nudge_y = -75,
    box.padding = unit(0.8, "lines"),
    point.padding = unit(0.4, "lines"),
    segment.colour = "grey40",
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  coord_brain(clip = "off") +
  theme_brain2()
```

Those last two are aesthetics rather than arguments, which matters when you want one label to shout and the others to stay quiet.
Map them and each connector gets its own treatment.

```{r}
#| label: accent
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Left lateral view of the dk atlas with three names outside the
#|   outline. Superior frontal is in dark red with a thick red line, while
#|   temporal pole and lateral occipital are in grey with thin grey lines.
#| fig-cap: >
#|   One region accented and the others kept quiet, by mapping the
#|   connector's colour and width.
regions <- data.frame(
  label = c("lh_superiorfrontal", "lh_temporalpole", "lh_lateraloccipital"),
  accent = c("firebrick", "grey60", "grey60"),
  weight = c(1.5, 0.4, 0.4)
)

ggplot() +
  geom_brain(
    atlas = dk(), hemi = "left", view = "lateral", show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_brain_text(
    data = regions,
    aes(
      colour = accent,
      segment.colour = accent,
      segment.linewidth = weight
    ),
    nudge_x = c(-70, -40, 90),
    nudge_y = c(70, -55, -20),
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  coord_brain(clip = "off") +
  theme_brain2()
```

Neither of them is scaled, so map them to a column that already holds the values you want drawn.
That is why `accent` above is a column of colour names rather than a grouping variable, and why the text colour needs `scale_colour_identity()` while the connector does not.

## When there is more than one view

With the default layout a region shows up in every view that draws it, and it gets named in each one.
You still only write the nudge once.
One row of your data is one nudge, however many anchors that row turns into, so the name moves the same way everywhere.

```{r}
#| label: multi-view
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Four views of the left hemisphere side by side. The insula is named in
#|   the three views that show it, each name nudged downwards by the same
#|   amount, and left unnamed in the view where it is hidden.
#| fig-cap: >
#|   One written row, one nudge, applied in every view that draws the region.
#| fig.height: 3
ggplot() +
  geom_brain(atlas = dk(), hemi = "left", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_brain_text(
    data = data.frame(label = "lh_insula"),
    nudge_y = -45,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  coord_brain(clip = "off") +
  theme_brain2()
```

## Where to go next

If what you want is to name the views rather than the regions inside them — "lateral", "medial" and so on — that is `annotate_brain()`, which `vignette("positioning-views")` covers.

And if your labels are fighting each other, the honest answer is usually to name fewer regions rather than to nudge harder.
Nudging is good for picking out the handful of regions a figure is actually about.
It will not rescue a plot that is trying to name everything at once.
